tour.title: Arashiyama: Bamboo, River & Mountain Temples
tour.summary: A river crossing, a troop of wild macaques, a Zen garden that outlived its temple, a bamboo plantation, a film star's hillside estate and one quiet moss temple — south to north in half a day.
tour.overviewText:
Arashiyama is where Kyoto runs out of city. The Katsura River pushes out of a gorge, spreads wide and shallow between wooded hills, and for roughly a thousand years this valley was the imperial court's back garden. Almost everything here is that history, reused.

Start with the Heian court, the imperial government that ruled from Kyoto between 794 and 1185. Emperors and nobles kept villas at Sagano, the district on the north bank, and came out to boat and watch the moon. Emperor Saga had a palace here in the 9th century. Emperor Kameyama retired to the same ground and is said to have watched the moon travel over the river and called it the clear moon crossing over — which gave the bridge its name, Togetsukyo, the Moon Crossing Bridge. A princess chosen to represent the emperor at Ise Shrine, Shinto's holiest site, purified herself for a year at Nonomiya, beside today's bamboo path.

Then politics arrived. In 1339 Ashikaga Takauji, the warlord who had just founded the Muromachi shogunate — the military government that then ruled Japan for two and a half centuries — built Tenryu-ji on the site of Kameyama's palace, for the spirit of Emperor Go-Daigo, the emperor he had fought, beaten and sent into exile. Tenryu-ji was ranked first of the Five Mountains: the shogunate's league table of Kyoto's Zen temples. State power, dressed as piety. The garden behind its halls was laid out by the monk Muso Soseki and survived every fire that took the buildings.

Faith here is layered, and this walk crosses both kinds. Nonomiya is Shinto — the older Japanese religion of kami, gods or spirits resident in particular places — and the shrine's business is purification. Tenryu-ji and Jojakko-ji are Buddhist, of two very different schools: Rinzai Zen, which trusts sitting meditation over scripture, and Nichiren, which centres on a single sutra.

What pays for Arashiyama now is visitors. It is one of Kyoto's most popular districts, and the local arguments about crowded buses, litter and carved bamboo are arguments about the cost of being loved. The bamboo is a working crop, and the woods at the foot of the mountain, once Tenryu-ji's land, have been protected scenic forest since the Meiji era.

The walk runs south to north: river first, then the monkey hill, the Zen garden, the bamboo, an actor's estate and a quiet hillside temple. It measures about 2.2 kilometres between stops, roughly 35 minutes of walking, plus the climb up and down the monkey hill. Spread that over half a day: most of your hours go to standing still in gardens.

Practicals. Wear shoes you can climb in: the monkey hill and both hillside temples are steps and packed earth, not pavements. Late January and early February are properly cold, often 0°C to 10°C, with bare maples and the year's best light on the river. Temples close between 16:30 and 17:00, so start by nine. Prices are in yen (¥); carry cash, because the monkey park takes nothing else. And one warning for this season: the Sagano Romantic Train does not run from late December to the end of February.

Buy a coffee, walk back over the bridge and look upstream — the hills you just climbed are the reason this place was anything at all.
tour.difficulty: Easy to moderate. Flat riverside and shopping street at the start, then a stiff 120-metre climb at the monkey park and steep stepped paths up to Okochi Sanso and Jojakko-ji. Rough, uneven ground with many steps; not step-free anywhere after the river.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start at first light, around 7:30 to 8:00. The bamboo lane is a free public path open at all hours and is nearly empty before the shops open, and the low morning sun is the best light the river gets all year. Temples open at 8:30 to 9:00 and close between 16:30 and 17:00, so an 8am start fits everything in comfortably. Weekends matter at Tenryu-ji: the cloud-dragon hall opens on Saturdays, Sundays and holidays only outside the spring and autumn special exhibitions. Late January and early February are cold and quiet — dress for a hillside, not a city street.

stops.name: Togetsukyo Bridge
stops.narration:
Stop on the bridge and look upstream, where the water comes out of the gorge. You are standing on the most photographed object in western Kyoto, and it is a fake — in the best possible sense.

Togetsukyo means Moon Crossing Bridge. The name is usually credited to Emperor Kameyama, who kept his retirement palace on the far bank in the late 13th century and is said to have watched the moon travel over the water and remarked that it looked like the clear moon crossing the bridge. In 1346 the Zen master Muso Soseki, the monk who designed the garden you will see further up this walk, listed the bridge as one of Tenryu-ji's ten finest views and gave it the name it still carries.

The structure under your feet is from 1934: 155 metres long, 12.2 metres wide, a steel-reinforced concrete girder bridge. Only the railing is wood — hinoki cypress, in a lattice pattern. Look along the deck: the road humps about a metre in the middle, a deliberate echo of the arched wooden bridges that stood here before, so that from the bank the concrete reads as timber. The first bridge at this crossing is attributed to a monk named Dōshō, said to have built it in the 830s to serve Hōrin-ji temple on the south bank, which is why for centuries it was called Hōrinji-bashi. It burned in the Ōnin War, the 1467 to 1477 civil war that flattened most of Kyoto, and was rebuilt in 1479 on donations. In 1606 a merchant named Suminokura Ryōi cleared the gorge upstream to open the river to log and cargo boats, and moved the bridge to this spot.

Here is the thing most people miss. What you are standing on is only half a bridge. Togetsukyo crosses to the island in the middle of the river, Nakanoshima; a second, smaller bridge, Togetsu-kobashi, carries you the last stretch to the south bank. Look back at the far end and you can see the join.

Two more things. First, this water changes name as it runs: Ōi-gawa in its upper reach above the gorge, Hozu-gawa through the gorge itself, Katsura-gawa from here down toward the sea. Same river, three names. Second, at night this bridge is lit by a small hydroelectric generator installed in 2005 at the West Takase diversion just upstream; the surplus power is sold and the money pays for cleaning the banks. And one piece of local folklore, from the 13th-birthday pilgrimage to Hōrin-ji: do not look back over your shoulder until you have finished crossing, or the wisdom the temple granted you is said to be revoked.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. The bridge is a public road and is open at all hours, lit after dark by the hydro generator upstream.
stops.openingHours: Open at all hours, every day. Lit in the evening.
stops.accessibility: Level deck with a stone-paved footway raised one step above the roadway on each side, and a gentle hump at the middle. Fine with wheels if you keep to the footway; the kerb is the only obstacle.
stops.insiderTip: Walk to the middle and look upstream in the morning, when the sun comes down the gorge and lights the water. Then check the far end of the deck: you can see where Togetsukyo ends at the island and the smaller Togetsu-kobashi begins.
stops.nextStopDirections: From the bridge, carry on to the far bank — Togetsukyo only reaches the island in mid-river, so keep going over the smaller Togetsu-kobashi to the south shore. Walk about twenty metres along the bank, past the small torii gate of Ichitani Munakata Shrine, and the ticket window of the monkey park is on your left.

stops.name: Iwatayama Monkey Park
stops.narration:
A gate marks the bottom of a hill, and the first honest thing to say is that this is a climb: about 120 metres of ascent, fifteen to twenty minutes, on a path of steps, packed earth and one loose gravel stretch. There is no lift and no shortcut. Wear shoes with grip, take it slowly, and remember that the payoff is at the top.

The animals are Japanese macaques — nihonzaru — the only monkey species native to Japan and the northernmost-living non-human primate on earth. Around 140 of them live in a single troop on this slope, wild and free to leave. They do leave: most nights they head up the mountain to sleep, which is why the park sometimes shuts early. And if you came expecting monkeys soaking in a hot spring, that photograph is of a different troop, in Nagano, far to the north-east.

They stay close because they are fed here. At the summit hut you buy bags of fruit and nuts and push them through a wire grille to the monkeys clustered on the other side. Understand the arrangement: the humans are the ones indoors, behind bars, and the monkeys are loose. It is a neat inversion, and it exists for a reason. Feeding by hand teaches wild animals that human hands mean food, and that is how you get bitten visitors and dead monkeys. So the rules are strict and they are not decoration: do not touch, do not feed by hand, do not bring your own food, no pets, no drones.

Watch the troop for a while and you will start to see structure. Macaques live in ranked societies — dominant males, and females whose status is inherited rather than earned — with alliances, quarrels and a great deal of grooming, which is less affection than social accounting. Watch who eats first and who gets groomed by whom.

The viewpoint sits at about 155 metres, above the river, and it is worth the climb even if monkeys bore you. Below you are Togetsukyo, the shopping street, and the whole bowl of Arashiyama; in winter the hills behind the town are sharp and clear. This is the angle painters used for the district's standard portrait.

Tickets are ¥800 for adults (16 and over), ¥400 for children aged 4 to 15, free under three — and cash only, in yen, no cards, so have notes ready before you reach the gate. The park is open roughly 9:00 to 16:30 with last tickets around 16:00, closed on 1 January and on days of heavy rain or snow. Verify the day's closing time at the gate: in winter the monkeys decide it for you. Then come down, cross both bridges back to the north bank, and walk up the shopping street to the Zen temple.
stops.entranceFeeNote: ¥800 for adults (16+), ¥400 for children 4 to 15, free under three. Cash only and Japanese yen only — no cards, no IC transit cards. Verify at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Typically 9:00 to 16:30, with last tickets around 16:00, but the staff close early when the monkeys head back up the mountain. Closed 1 January and on days of heavy rain or snow. Confirm on the day.
stops.accessibility: Not accessible, honestly: a 120-metre climb on a rough path with long flights of steps and one loose gravel section. No lift. The summit viewing area itself is mostly level.
stops.insiderTip: You are the one behind bars at the summit hut — the monkeys are loose and the wire grille is there to stop you feeding them by hand. Buy a bag of food, sit down inside and watch the troop's hierarchy sort itself out. And climb for the view as much as the animals: the river and the whole district are laid out below.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk back down the hill, recross both bridges to the north bank, and follow the shopping street north — Randen Arashiyama tram station is on your right. Tenryu-ji's main gate is on the left at the top of the street, about a kilometre, fifteen minutes on foot, from the park gate.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Hyppolyte de Saint-Rambert, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Tenryu-ji
stops.narration:
Tenryu-ji is a Zen temple, so start with what Zen is. Zen is a school of Buddhism — the religion founded on the Buddha's teaching that life is marked by suffering, and that suffering has a cause which can be ended. Zen's particular claim is that this is understood by sitting still and looking directly at your own mind rather than by studying scripture. Rinzai Zen, the branch here, also uses koans: riddle-like problems, such as the sound of one hand clapping, designed to exhaust logic and force a different kind of attention. Keep that in mind when you look at the garden, because in Zen a garden is not decoration. It is a device for concentrating the mind.

The temple was founded in 1339 by Ashikaga Takauji, the warlord who had just set up the Muromachi shogunate — the military government that ran Japan from Kyoto for the next two and a half centuries. He built it for the spirit of Emperor Go-Daigo, the emperor he had fought, defeated and sent into exile in Yoshino, where he died. A temple for a rival's ghost is piety, and it is also public relations.

The site was not chosen at random. This was Kameyama-dono, the retirement palace of the Emperor Kameyama who gave the bridge its name, and it was converted into a temple in 1342. Tenryu-ji means Temple of the Heavenly Dragon. It was ranked first of the Five Mountains — the Kyoto Gozan, the shogunate's official league table of Rinzai Zen temples, which was a way of organising, and controlling, the country's most powerful religious institutions. It is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site as part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto.

The buildings you see are mostly Meiji-era, from the late 19th century: fire took the earlier ones, repeatedly. The garden is the survivor. It was laid out by Musō Soseki, a monk who was the temple's first abbot, an adviser to the shogunate and the finest garden designer of his age. His Sōgenchi garden borrows the Arashiyama hills as a backdrop — shakkei, 'borrowed scenery', the trick of composing a garden so that a mountain you do not own becomes part of it — and centres on a pond traditionally said to trace the shape of the character for heart-mind. Seven hundred years of fires, and the garden is essentially as he left it.

Two extras are worth the money. The temple buildings, ¥300 on top of the garden's ¥500, put you on the tatami of the Hōjō and Shoin, where the garden is framed like a hanging scroll. And the Hattō, the Dharma Hall, holds a cloud dragon painted on its ceiling in 1997 by Kayama Matazō for the 650th anniversary of Musō's death: 159 cypress planks, a nine-metre circle of white plaster, and a dragon in happō-nirami, 'glaring in eight directions', meaning it seems to watch you wherever you stand. That costs another ¥500 and is open on Saturdays, Sundays and holidays outside the spring and autumn special exhibitions — so in late winter, plan a weekend. The hall is closed on 2 January 2027 and during ceremonies, and a fragment of the earlier dragon, painted by Suzuki Shōnen in the Meiji era, is displayed in the Daihōjō every February.

Hours are 8:30 to 17:00 with last entry at 16:50, and tickets are sold at the garden gate, the main building and the north gate. Verify prices and closures at the window — restoration and ceremonies move them.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Garden ¥500. Add ¥300 for the temple buildings (¥800 total). Add a further ¥500 for the Hattō and its cloud-dragon ceiling, open weekends and holidays outside the spring and autumn exhibitions. Verify at the window.
stops.openingHours: Daily, 8:30 to 17:00, last entry 16:50. The Hattō (cloud dragon) is usually open 9:00 to 16:30 on Saturdays, Sundays and holidays only, with daily openings during spring and autumn special exhibitions. Confirm on the day.
stops.accessibility: The garden path is gravel and packed earth with gentle slopes and a few shallow steps; a wheelchair can manage the main loop with help. The temple buildings involve raised tatami floors, thresholds and stairs, and are not step-free.
stops.insiderTip: Sit on the veranda of the Hōjō and look for the borrowed scenery: the garden's pond is designed so that the Arashiyama hills become part of the composition. If it is a weekend in winter, pay the extra ¥500 for the cloud dragon in the Hattō — and remember the dragon is only twenty-nine years old, not medieval.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave by Tenryu-ji's north gate, cross the lane and you are at the foot of the bamboo path beside Nonomiya Shrine. Walk north up the lane between the culms; the grove runs for several hundred metres to the top of the hill.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Daderot, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Sagano Bamboo Grove
stops.narration:
You are in a plantation, not a forest, and that is the first thing worth knowing. This is mōsō bamboo, Phyllostachys edulis — a giant bamboo species native to China, brought to Japan centuries ago and grown here as a crop. Bamboo is a grass, not a tree: those tall green stems are culms, the joints are nodes, and a whole clump is one connected root system. Mōsō is the fastest-growing plant on earth; in the shooting season, from late April into May, a new culm can add around a metre in a single day. If you are lucky you hear it — a creak, then a crack.

Japan's environment ministry counts the grove's sound among the country's soundscapes: wind in the leaves, thousands of culms knocking against each other, the crunch of the path underfoot. It is the one thing a photograph cannot carry, so stand still for a minute and listen instead of filming.

What the grove produces is money. In spring the young shoots — takenoko, braised with rice or grilled over charcoal — are dug and sold as a delicacy. Cut culms become fences, baskets, sieves, brooms, chopsticks, tea whisks, scaffolding and flutes. The families who own these plots harvest them on rotation, because bamboo cut at the wrong time of year splits and beetles. And bamboo is not immortal: a stand flowers once in a very long interval, decades or more, sets seed and dies. That is why the grove you are walking through is tended rather than wild.

The path itself, Take-no-michi — the bamboo lane — is a free public road running between Tenryu-ji's north gate and the temples further up the valley. No ticket, no gate, open at all hours. That is also its problem. Between about ten in the morning and four in the afternoon it is one of the most crowded lanes in Japan, a slow procession of people photographing the same empty stretch of path. Come before eight, in the half-light, and you can have it. Come after dark and you will have it entirely — it is unlit, genuinely black, and the wind is much louder. And do not carve anything into a culm. Visitors have done it often enough to be a standing local grievance, and bamboo does not heal.

At the south end of the lane, beside Tenryu-ji's north gate, stands Nonomiya Shrine. The name means 'shrine in the field'. In the Heian period, when an imperial princess was chosen as saiō — the unmarried woman who would serve as the emperor's representative at Ise Shrine, the holiest site in Shinto, the older Japanese religion of kami, gods or spirits resident in particular places — she had to purify herself here for a year or more before making the journey. Each time, the shrine's exact site was fixed anew by divination. Nonomiya appears in the tenth chapter of The Tale of Genji and in a Noh play by Zeami, and the saigū procession is reenacted along the river every year. Stop at the black torii on your way through: it is free, it takes two minutes, and it is the oldest story on this walk.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. The lane is a public path with no gate and no ticket, open at all hours. Nonomiya Shrine at the south end is also free.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times, every day. Unlit after dark. Busiest from roughly 10:00 to 16:00.
stops.accessibility: A gently sloping lane of packed earth and gravel, with some uneven patches and no steps. Manageable with wheels in dry weather; muddy and slick after rain.
stops.insiderTip: The lane has no gate, so you can walk it out of order: come back at 7:30 in the morning and you will have the whole grove to yourself. Then step two minutes south to Nonomiya Shrine, where Heian princesses were purified before being sent to serve at Ise.
stops.nextStopDirections: Keep walking north up the lane to its top end, where the path bends and the bamboo opens out. On the left you will see a gate with a small ticket window and a flight of stone steps behind it: that is Okochi Sanso, the next stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Basile Morin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Okochi Sanso Villa
stops.narration:
At the top of the bamboo lane a gate opens onto a private hill, and the story here is about a man who turned film fame into a garden. Ōkōchi Denjirō, 1896 to 1962, was the biggest star of jidaigeki — Japanese period films, the samurai costume dramas that were the country's most popular cinema from the 1920s to the 1950s. He bought this slope on the back of Mt. Ogura, behind Tenryu-ji, and spent roughly thirty years building a villa on it: about two hectares, near enough five acres, with a main house, tea houses, a Buddhist hall, a small shrine and a museum devoted to his own career. He was still building when he died, and his family opened the place to the public.

The scale is the point. Two hectares of hillside, terraced and planted by hand, with maples, pines, moss and bamboo fencing, and paths that climb in stages so that the view arrives a piece at a time.

Four structures here are registered as national Tangible Cultural Properties — the designation Japan gives buildings worth keeping. The Daijōkaku, the main house, deliberately mixes two architectural registers: shoin-zukuri, the formal style of samurai and temple reception rooms, and sukiya-zukuri, the lighter, more rustic style developed for tea houses. The Tekisuian is the tea house. The Jibutsudō, a small Buddhist hall, is a Meiji-era building brought here from elsewhere. The Chūmon is the middle gate you walk through. The buildings are viewed from outside only; the interiors are not open.

Climb to the upper viewpoint. From up here you get the Hozu gorge, the Arashiyama hills, the city below and, on a clear winter day, Mt. Hiei away to the north-east — the mountain whose temples were traditionally held to guard Kyoto from the unlucky north-east direction. The garden was designed so that something is in season every month. In late January and February that means evergreens, moss, the bare architecture of the maples, camellia, and the shape of the ground itself, which leaves usually hide.

The ticket is around ¥1,000 and includes a bowl of matcha at the tea house near the top. Matcha is powdered green tea — the whole leaf, stone-ground, whisked into hot water with a bamboo whisk rather than steeped and strained, which is why it is opaque and bitter. In a garden tea house the point is the pause rather than the caffeine. Sit down, look at the view, and let the small sweet that comes with it cut the bitterness; check at the gate whether the sweet is still included, because it has come and gone over the years.

Open roughly 9:00 to 17:00 with last entry in the late afternoon, and no fixed closing days. Verify at the gate — this is a private estate run as a museum, and its calendar is its own.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Around ¥1,000, which includes a bowl of matcha at the tea house. A sweet has historically come with it but has been dropped and reinstated over the years — check at the gate. Verify the price and opening times on the day.
stops.openingHours: Typically open daily, roughly 9:00 to 17:00, with last entry in the late afternoon. Confirm on the day — this is a private estate with its own calendar.
stops.accessibility: Not accessible, honestly: steep stepped paths climbing a hillside in stages, uneven stone and gravel, and no lift. There is a shorter route to the tea house if you ask at the gate.
stops.insiderTip: Take the matcha at the tea house near the top and sit with it rather than drinking it standing up — the ticket exists to buy you that pause. Then find the small museum to Ōkōchi and look at what a film fortune bought in pre-war Japan.
stops.nextStopDirections: Come back down through the gate and turn right along the lane, heading north-west. The little Torokko Arashiyama station of the Sagano railway is a couple of minutes along it, and Jojakko-ji's thatched gate is on the left about five minutes beyond that, where the lane curves between the hillside temples.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: KimonBerlin, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Jojakko-ji
stops.narration:
From the crowds to silence. Jojakko-ji is a small temple on the slope of Mt. Ogura that makes no effort to impress you, which is what makes the story behind its name worth the climb.

This is a Nichiren Buddhist temple. Nichiren was a 13th-century Japanese monk who taught that the essential truth of Buddhism is contained in one scripture, the Lotus Sutra, and that the way to liberation is to chant its title: Nam-myōhō-renge-kyō, which means, roughly, devotion to the Lotus Sutra of the Wonderful Law. Nichiren's followers were famously confrontational in his lifetime and were persecuted for it; the school survived and is one of the largest in Japan today. The temple's name comes from the jōjakkō-dō, the Land of Tranquil Light — the realm of pure radiance where, in the Lotus Sutra, the eternal Buddha teaches. The founders looked at this hillside and thought it resembled that.

They were the monk Nisshin, sixteenth abbot of Honkoku-ji in Kyoto, and his patron Enju-in, and the year was 1596 — the tail end of a century of civil war, a good moment for a scholar to retire to a hill. The main hall was moved here from the guest quarters of Fushimi Castle with the help of a warlord, Kobayakawa Hideaki, whose career is a reminder that the 1590s rewarded opportunism. The bell tower was rebuilt in 1642; its bell was melted down for metal during the Second World War and a new one was cast in 1973.

Climb the stone steps — this is a hillside temple, and the paths are steps, moss and tree roots, uneven and slippery after rain — and look for three things.

First, the Niō gate: a thatched-roof gate moved here in 1616 from Honkoku-ji, with two fierce guardian figures, Niō, flanking the entrance. Tradition attributes them to Unkei, the greatest sculptor of Japanese Buddhist images, though the actual carver is unknown. They are said to cure ailments of the legs and hips, which is why worshippers have hung straw sandals, waraji, on the wall beside them. Look at the wall; the sandals are the offering.

Second, the tahōtō, the two-storey pagoda rising above the maples. It was built in 1620, stands about twelve metres tall, and is an Important Cultural Property — a national listing. In February, with the maples bare, you can see its full shape; in autumn it is half-hidden in red.

Third, the view. From the upper grounds the whole of Sagano opens below you, and on a cold clear morning you can see the gorge the river comes out of. The temple also keeps a wheeled koto, a kind of zither, said to have been given by Emperor Takakura to Lady Kogo — the court beauty whose tomb stands near the bridge you started at. It was donated here by Kobayakawa Hideaki, which ties this quiet hill back to the politics of the castle he helped to build.

Admission is ¥600, open 9:00 to 17:00 with last entry at 16:30, and there are no closing days. Some guidebooks still print ¥500, so verify at the gate.
stops.entranceFeeNote: ¥600, per the temple's own notice. Some guidebooks still print ¥500, so verify at the gate. No closing days.
stops.openingHours: Daily, 9:00 to 17:00, last entry 16:30. No closing days. Occasional special openings of the main hall are announced separately.
stops.accessibility: Not accessible: long flights of stone steps up a hillside, moss-covered and uneven, with roots across the path. Slippery after rain. The lower gate and a short stretch beyond it are the only level ground.
stops.insiderTip: Find the straw sandals hung on the wall by the Niō gate — worshippers leave them because the guardian figures are said to heal legs and hips. Then walk to the upper grounds and look back down over Sagano: on a clear winter morning this is the quietest good view in Arashiyama.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk, and you are high on the hillside above Sagano with the afternoon in front of you. Carry on north up the lane for ten minutes and you reach Saga-Toriimoto, a preserved street of Meiji-era machiya townhouses, and beyond it two very different hillside temples: Adashino Nenbutsu-ji, where hundreds of small stone markers for the forgotten dead stand among bamboo, and Otagi Nenbutsu-ji, whose 1,200 carved stone rakan — the Buddha's followers — each have their own face, made by amateur sculptors in the 1980s and 1990s. For the train, walk back down to Arashiyama: JR Saga-Arashiyama station is about twenty-five minutes on foot, and the ride back to Kyoto Station takes fifteen minutes for around ¥240, while the Randen tram to central Kyoto leaves from the middle of the shopping street. If you want the river trip, the Hozugawa boat runs all winter from Kameoka — heated flat-bottomed boats, two hours down the gorge, ¥6,000, last departures in mid-afternoon — so ride the JR line out to Kameoka on another morning and float back to the bridge you started at. And note for this season: the Sagano Romantic Train does not run between late December and the end of February, so check the operator's calendar before you build a day around it.
